islam-religion-of-peace: The phrase "religion of peace" now reaches most readers as sarcasm, under news of violence done in Islam's name. We set out four things the sources contain: a name rooted in peace, a universal prohibition on killing, a rejection of forced belief and rules of war that restrain the victor. We then face the violence that produced the sarcasm. Our verdict is that the violence contradicts the sources, that the contradiction can be shown from the sources themselves, and that the sources came first.
prophet-died-poisoning: Critics argue that the poisoned meal at Khaybar shows God did not protect the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), so he was no prophet. We answer in six points from the early biographies and the hadith. The sources record a man who was warned, stopped the meal and lived four more years, completing a mission the Quran marks as finished. The promise of protection in 5:67 concerned the delivery of the message. No verse promises a prophet that he cannot be hurt.
muhammad-false-prophet-claim: One critique holds that Muhammad (peace be upon him) failed the test of earlier prophets: no spectacle, a failed prophecy about Byzantium and an experience better explained as epilepsy. We take each part at its strongest. The Quran withholds the showy sign and says why. The hadith add named miracle reports. The Byzantine prophecy named the right losers and winners within its window. The epilepsy theory traces to Byzantine polemic and fails the clinical record. The claim that no evidence was offered does not survive the sources.
did-muhammad-perform-miracles: Critics quote verses in which the Prophet (peace be upon him) refuses a demanded sign and conclude that he had no credentials. We give six answers. The Quran records the refusals and explains them, and the Gospels show Jesus refusing signs on the same terms. The Quran presents itself as the Prophet's sign, reports the splitting of the moon, and the companions report further signs. Moses, Jesus and Muhammad all taught that wonders can mislead and that the message is what must be weighed.
al-zutt-allegation: A narration in the Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal says jinn, compared to the people of al-Zutt, crowded around the Prophet (peace be upon him) as he recited. A recent English reading turns its verb, yarkabun, into "sexual assault". We examine the verb's range, the anatomy the text describes, the occasion, the history of the claim and the grading of the report. The editors of the Musnad grade this cluster weak. The allegation picks the worst sense of one word and reads it into a report its own tradition questions.
islamic-dilemma: The "Islamic dilemma" says the Quran affirms the Torah and the Gospel, so either they were intact and contradict the Quran, or corrupt and the Quran praised books no one could follow. We show that the argument needs five assumptions: that the Injil is the four gospels, that corruption is all or nothing, that distortion is only textual, that the Quran defers to the earlier books and that a situational command is universal. Any one failing opens a third option: real revelations, a mixed record, and the Quran as their criterion.
does-islam-teach-the-bible-was-corrupted: Christian apologists claim that Islam endorsed the Bible as Christians hold it and that the charge of corruption came later. We grade seven points of Muslim evidence. Three are firm: the Quran charges falsification, Ibn Abbas said the text was changed, and the classical scholars held that some wording changed. Four are thin. No verse lists which passages changed, so the Quran is the criterion over the earlier books. Islam neither endorses the Bible as it stands nor calls it a forgery.
christian-twin-of-the-islamic-dilemma: The "Islamic dilemma" tests the Quran against the earlier books. We apply the same test to the New Testament, which affirms the Hebrew Bible and departs from it, and grade seven points. Five are firm, among them the early Christian awareness of the gap and the old practice of reading earlier scripture by a later authority. The twin is real in structure: a test that sinks both books tests neither. It cannot show that the Quran is true, and the Christian and Jewish replies still stand.
quran-verses-on-torah-and-gospel: Both sides quote a few verses on the Torah and the Gospel and declare the matter closed. We read seven claims slowly and grade each. Five are moderate, including that no verse says the earlier books were preserved, that 5:43 speaks of a Torah in Medina, and that the command to judge by the Gospel does not vouch for every line. Two are thin. The verses fit al Faruqi's reading, that the earlier books have a divine base and a human history, without proving it.
early-christians-charged-others-with-cor: The charge that another community corrupted its scripture can sound late and sectarian. We show from seven points that it was ordinary in the first four Christian centuries. Justin charged the Jews, Celsus charged the Christians, the church charged Marcion, and the Pseudo-Clementines spoke of false passages. The manuscripts of Mark and John show what such growth looked like. A charge proves nothing by being made, and it needs manuscripts, witnesses or a revealed criterion.
quran-word-kitab-meanings: Much of the argument about the Quran and the earlier books turns on the word kitab, "book". We sort its Quranic uses into seven points: a decree, the heavenly Book, the revelation itself and the pages people copy. Four points are firm and three are moderate, and 3:93 stays a real difficulty. The question "does the Quran affirm the Book they have" needs a second question, which meaning of Book a verse intends, and a reading verse by verse answers it better than a slogan.
trinity-in-the-hebrew-bible-tested: Christians read the Hebrew Bible as pointing to a God who is one in three, and Jews and Muslims read it as pointing to a God who is one. We test seven claims against the Hebrew wording. The Angel of the Lord passages are the strongest Christian case. The plural of Genesis 1:26, Isaiah 9:6, the Spirit and Zechariah are open readings that the same pages can answer. The Hebrew Bible states that God is one and nowhere states that he is three.
who-is-the-holy-spirit: For most Christians the Holy Spirit is God, the third person of the Trinity. For Muslims Ruh al-Qudus is a created being, the angel Gabriel. We give seven answers from the Quran and the Bible. The Quran uses the name consistently and ascribes the same act to the Spirit and to Gabriel, and Luke names the same messenger to Mary. The Hebrew Bible speaks of God's spirit as His power. The full deity of the Spirit was defined only in 381.
matthew-fulfilment-quotations-checked: Matthew says again and again that events happened "to fulfil" the prophets, and Muslim readers are told this proves more about Jesus than the Quran says. We set eight of his citations beside the passages they cite. Six differ firmly in wording or setting, Isaiah 7:14 is firm on context, and Isaiah 42 is moderate. In each case Matthew reads the older text in the light of Jesus. His "fulfilment" is a way of reading, close to the Qumran commentaries, and yields no list of predictions.
five-pillars-explained: Most introductions to Islam list the five pillars and stop. We explain each one: its meaning, the text that commands it, what it asks of a person on an ordinary day and the question an outsider is most likely to ask. The list comes from the hadith of Gabriel. Read in order, the pillars form a shape: belief, a daily practice that keeps it in view, money, a month of fasting and a single pilgrimage. Together they are the minimum structure the tradition asks of every Muslim.
before-you-convert-to-islam: A list on social media tells a would-be convert to meet a set of "roles" before taking the testimony of faith. We answer it in seven points. A person enters Islam by the testimony alone, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) taught practice in stages and forbade the extremism the list recommends. The list is right on pork, intoxicants, gambling, prayer and fasting, and leaves out the exemptions. Its rules on dogs, tattoos and circumcision overstate or invent what the sources say.
who-is-allah: Allah is the Arabic word for God, used by Muslims and by Arabic-speaking Christians. We answer five misunderstandings about the name: that it names a different god, that it was a moon god, that this God is remote, and that Muslims worship Muhammad (peace be upon him). Each fails against the sources. The Quran forbids worship of the moon, addresses Jews and Christians as worshippers of one God, fills its pages with names of mercy and calls its messenger a mortal man.
is-allah-a-deceiver-makr: Critics translate 3:54 as "God is the best of deceivers" and argue that nothing God says can then be trusted. We give seven answers on the word makr. It means a hidden plan, good or bad by its aim. In every verse where it is used of God, it answers a plot made by others, against Jesus, Muhammad (peace be upon him), Salih or the message. The commentators read it as requital named after the deed, and the Bible uses stronger language of God.
universe-demands-creator: The atheist account of origins comes in three forms: the universe is a brute fact, it caused itself, or it is one of countless universes. We state the best reply to each and show five places where the account must say "it just is". None of the five is a proof. Together they point to a necessary, powerful and intelligent cause, and Muslims find the further description of that cause in revelation, where the Quran places reflection on creation at the start of faith.
why-does-god-allow-suffering: The argument from suffering asks why a merciful God allows children to suffer and the strong to hurt the weak. We give six points from the Islamic sources and say where they stop. One is firm: the Quran's own prophets suffer, so pain is no proof of God's absence. Four are moderate: the test, the promise of ease, free will and the meaning given to pain. The sources give no full explanation, and they ask the community to relieve suffering where it can.
morality-without-god: Secular humanists are often decent people. We ask whether their account of why anyone should be decent holds together, and state four points with the humanist reply to each. At each point the secular account borrows what it cannot supply: obligation, a standard above consensus, a reason to rank one impulse over another and a goal for progress. The replies describe how people behave and leave obligation unexplained. Goodness needs a ground, and the search for one leads to a lawgiver.
instruments-islamic-world: The usual story makes the Muslim world a warehouse that kept Greek science until Europe reopened it. We describe six instruments that show invention: the alembic, the camera obscura, al-Zahrawi's surgical forceps, the astrolabe's projection, the torquetum and their successors. Several began as answers to a religious need, such as the hour of prayer or the direction of Mecca. The torquetum and the Jabirian writings are disputed, and the rest of the case stands without them.
seven-libraries: A library takes generations to gather and one season to scatter. We trace seven libraries of the Muslim world, from Baghdad to Timbuktu, and how each ended. Baghdad fell to invaders. Cordoba and Cairo were broken up by their own rulers and soldiers. The Nizamiyya faded, al-Qarawiyyin was saved by a restoration, the Suleymaniye was kept whole, and Timbuktu's manuscripts were mostly rescued in our own time. Libraries survive while someone pays to keep them.
deuteronomy-prophecy-and-the-paraclete: The Quran says Muhammad (peace be upon him) is written in the books of the People of the Book, and Muslims point to Deuteronomy 18 and the Comforter in John. We set out four points with the Christian objection to each. The Muslim reading rests on the comparison with Moses, the Torah's use of "brethren", John's evidence that the prophet was expected apart from the Christ, and "another" Comforter who comes after Jesus. The texts leave room for the argument, and the Muslim reading is old and careful.
same-god: Some Christians and some Muslims say that Allah of the Quran is a different god. We give seven reasons from the Quran why He is the same God. The Quran names the God of Jews and Christians as the God of Muslims, uses the shared Arabic name, claims the same prophets and criticises what is said about God without changing whom it addresses. The Trinity and the status of Jesus remain a serious disagreement, and such a disagreement presupposes one God spoken of by both.
jesus-not-god: Muslims hold that Jesus was born of a virgin, worked miracles, is the Messiah and will return. They do not hold that he was God. We give five reasons from the Christian sources: he prayed, said the Father was greater, did not know the hour and never plainly claimed the title. Christian replies to each verse depend on the doctrine of two natures, which the verses do not state. The Muslim reading needs the least added to the text.
where-did-jesus-say-he-is-god: Muslims ask for a verse where Jesus says "I am God, worship me", and a Christian reply turns the question around and asks Muslims for verses their practice relies on. We give six answers. The reply is right that doctrine draws on the whole of scripture. It fails on its own test: the Quran's Jesus calls himself God's servant, and the five gospel passages offered describe authority given to him, homage the Bible gives to kings and a unity he shares with his disciples.
did-jesus-pray-to-whom: The Gospels show Jesus praying before dawn, through the night and on his face in Gethsemane, and Muslims ask to whom God would pray. We give seven answers, stating the Christian reply fairly: he prayed in his human nature, as the councils of 451 and 681 defined. That doctrine was framed later to meet such passages, and it can absorb any passage at all. Read as they stand, the prayers are those of a servant to his Lord, as the Quran describes Jesus.
manuscript-transmission: Both Muslims and Christians claim that their scripture was reliably transmitted. We compare the Quran and the New Testament on five points: how each was passed on, how settled the text is, how close the oldest manuscripts stand to the events, what each admits was added, and what each community claims. The Quran has memorisation beside writing, a standard copy within a generation and no recognised interpolations. On the question of what the text says, the Muslim case is the stronger.
shared-prophets: The Quran tells the stories of the prophets as reminders to readers who already know them. We compare six figures shared with the Bible, five with all three faiths and Jesus with Christians alone. The men and most events are the same. The Quran's changes cluster around inherited sin, salvation by kinship and divine sonship, and each removes an idea later theology built on. Muslims read this as restoration, and many Jewish and Christian scholars read it as adaptation.
verses-read-differently: Most argument between Christians and Muslims comes down to a few verses that each side finds obvious. We take seven of them and state both readings as their own holders would. In every case the Christian reading needs the doctrine of two natures, or the Trinity, in place before the verse is read, while the Muslim reading needs only the verse and the Quran's account of Jesus. Christians answer that doctrine is the result of reading all the verses together. The burden lies with the side that brings a framework to the text.
haman-anachronism: Orientalists since the seventeenth century have called the Quran's Haman, minister to Pharaoh, a mix-up with the Haman of Esther, eight centuries later in Persia. We give five answers. The charge assumes that the two texts mean one figure and depends on the dates assigned to Moses. The Vienna door jamb shows the kind of office that existed in New Kingdom Egypt, and the Quran distinguishes Joseph's king from Moses' Pharaoh. A shared name can start a question and cannot settle one. The charge of error is unproven.
where-is-the-injil: Critics ask Muslims to produce the Injil the Quran says God gave Jesus. We give five answers. The challenge needs the Injil to be a lost book, the Quran to have promised its preservation, and judgement to fall on people for a text they never saw. The Quran says none of the three. It speaks of a revelation Jesus preached, attaches the promise of preservation to itself and ties judgement to what reached a person. Mark agrees that Jesus preached a gospel from God.
paul-and-the-law: Careful Christians hold that Paul changed the role of the Law while keeping its purpose, and that Jesus fulfilled the Law without cancelling it. We set Matthew 5:17 beside five sentences from the letters that bear Paul's name, each with its context and its best defence. Each can be defended alone. Read in order, they raise a plain question: would the Jesus of Matthew 5 have told a congregation that the Sabbath no longer bound them? The tension comes from inside the New Testament, and the Quran's Jesus fits the first saying.
paul-and-food-offered-to-idols: In a public debate a Muslim speaker asked who gave Paul the right to allow food offered to idols, when the apostles and the risen Jesus of Revelation forbade it. We give six answers. The Jerusalem decree called abstaining necessary, and Revelation condemns those who teach Christians to eat. Paul forbade temple meals and asked believers to spare a weaker brother, but held such food could be eaten, and never mentions the decree. The disagreement was real, and the Quran's food laws match the decree of James closely.
paul-claim-to-apostleship: Paul signed most of his letters with the claim that he was an apostle, and Christians have read the word as settling the matter. We ask six questions of the sources. Paul never met Jesus, rested his authority on a vision he alone reported, and records the suspicion of the apostles who had known Jesus. Communities that refused him lasted for centuries. A Christian may hold that Christ chose him, and that is a claim of faith. The historical claim that he spoke with the authority of Jesus rests on his word alone.
pauline-letters-authorship: Thirteen New Testament letters open with Paul's name. We set out six findings of Christian scholarship. Most critical scholars accept seven as his, some defend two more, and conservative scholars defend all thirteen. On the critical view the rest were written by others who wanted his authority, and Bart Ehrman argues that writers of the time called the practice lying. The New Testament was assembled with those letters inside it. The finding bears on the claim that the New Testament is what it says it is.
ezra-and-mary: Critics say the Quran misdescribes its neighbours when it says some Jews called Ezra the son of God and that Jesus will be asked whether he told people to take him and his mother as gods. We give five points. On Mary, the verse concerns what Jesus authorised and says nothing about Trinitarian doctrine, and the history of devotion to Mary gives it a plain context. On Ezra, the absence of a surviving text is real, and the answer rests on the first audience and Ezra's standing in Jewish memory.
aisha-sheep-report-stoning-and-suckling-: A report that a sheep ate a sheet holding verses is used to argue that the Quran lost verses by accident. We give five points on the report's chains and its classical readers. The sheep appears in one line of transmission, through a narrator trusted for history and doubted for law, and the stronger narrators leave it out. On A'isha's own words, the suckling verses were abrogated before the Prophet died, and the stoning ruling remained while its verse was withdrawn. Ibn Hazm and al-Baqillani answered the charge centuries ago.
seven-ahruf-cairo-edition-stoning-verse: Two arguments about the text of the Quran circulate together: that the seven modes the Prophet allowed make today's Quran one of seven, and that verses went missing, with the stoning verse as the best-known case. We answer both in ten points, from the reports on the seven modes to the ten readings and the 1924 Cairo edition. The modes and the readings are different things, and printings differ for known reasons. The scholars treat the stoning verse as wording withdrawn while its ruling stays, resting on the practice of the Prophet and his successors.
hafs-warsh-one-quran: A meme mocks Muslims for calling Hafs, Warsh, Qalun and twenty other printed editions one Quran. We give seven answers. The names are twenty transmitters of ten recognised readings, each tied by a chain to the Companions and bound to the written text of the Uthmanic copies. The Prophet approved recitation in more than one mode, and scholars recorded every difference. Most differences are vowels and dots, and the few that change a word say things the Quran affirms elsewhere. The readings are one Quran recited in recorded ways.
uthman-copies: Critics ask where the copies of the Quran that Uthman sent to the provinces around 650 have gone. We set out five facts. Two Birmingham leaves are radiocarbon dated early, a codex in Samarkand has long been named as Uthman's, and a first-century manuscript holds nearly half the Quran. They agree with the recited text in almost every detail. A few manuscripts, such as the lower text of the Sanaa palimpsest, carry variants that scholars still study. The sources report the burning of other copies and explain it.
qibla-change: Critics ask why the first Muslims prayed towards Jerusalem if Abraham and Ishmael built the Kaaba, and suggest the Mecca story came later. We give five facts. The first qibla is known from the Muslim sources themselves, which give the reason for the change, its date and the first reactions. The Quran records the change, names the objection it would draw and answers it. The hadith place the change early in Medina, and the architectural case for a later Mecca is weak.
why-five-prayers: A favourite challenge asks Muslims to show the five daily prayers from the Quran alone. We give five answers. The Quran gives the times of prayer, commands obedience to the Prophet and leaves the form to him. He prayed five times a day in public, and his community has done the same since. Zakah and the hajj follow the same pattern. The challenge works only for someone who has decided in advance that Islam must be Quran-only, and Islam never has been.
who-saw-gabriel: Critics note that Muhammad (peace be upon him) was alone in the cave and ask where the evidence for Gabriel is. We give five answers. No one else saw the burning bush, Isaiah's vision or the road to Damascus. Islam offers a text open to anyone, with a challenge attached. The sources report that people around the Prophet saw Gabriel in human form, and the first account of the call keeps a fear and doubt that an inventor would have left out. The claim is no less supported than other revelations.
fastest-growing-religion: The claim that Islam is the fastest-growing religion is a measurement, last published by the Pew Research Center in 2025. We set out six figures from the data. The growth comes from births, a young population and retention, and the latest decade confirms the trend Pew projected in 2015. Growth proves nothing about truth, and the Quran warns that following most of those on earth can lead a person astray. The figures describe the world accurately and show why a quarter of humanity's faith deserves to be understood.
arabic-words-science: Algebra, algorithm and the names of the stars came into European science from Arabic, mostly through translations made in Toledo and other Spanish cities in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. We trace six words and the route each took: through a book title, a scholar's name, a scribe's mistake and an Arabic word for a path. In each case the word crossed into Latin with the work that gave it meaning. The Arabic writers built on Greek and Indian sources, and they did the work Europe learned.
second-peter: Critics ask why Muslims should trust hadith written after the Prophet's death, when Muslims question gospels written decades after Jesus. We answer from the introduction to 2 Peter published by the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, in five entries. That introduction says another writer used Peter's name. A hadith comes with a named chain of transmitters, graded man by man, and the scholars rejected a great many reports. The major collections are ninth century, and early written pages survive to test them.
moon-craters: Many crater names on the Moon were given by Giovanni Riccioli in 1651 and adopted by the International Astronomical Union in 1935, and a striking number belong to astronomers who worked in Arabic. We describe six of them, with each crater and the work that earned it. These men corrected Ptolemy, measured the Earth and wrote the books Latin Europe learned its astronomy from, often under Latin names. Many worked on problems set by worship, such as the times of prayer and the direction of Mecca.
indonesia: The country with the most Muslims lies far from the Middle East, spread across thousands of islands. We set out six facts about Islam in Indonesia. It is a republic that names one God and recognises six religions, its national mosque faces a cathedral across a Jakarta street, and its two largest Muslim organisations can begin Ramadan on different days without crisis. Blasphemy prosecutions, restrictions on the Ahmadis and the violence of 1999 to 2002 are also on the record. The majority has handled its differences through law and negotiation.
ex-muslim-blog-study: In 2019 two researchers at Universiti Sultan Zainal Abidin published a study of a blog kept by a Malaysian woman who had left Islam. We summarise five findings on how she presented herself, told her story, persuaded readers and drew replies. The abuse of her opponents became part of her case. The replies that might reach her answered her reasons with respect. The study covers one blog, so it is suggestive only. It agrees with the Quran's call for wisdom, good counsel and the better reply.
kaaba-witnesses: Critics say no ancient source outside Islam mentions Mecca's sanctuary, and some defenders answer with every text that might. We weigh five witnesses. One is the Quran itself. Diodorus and Ptolemy may refer to the Kaaba and remain disputed, a recent inscription bears on the history of its name, and the psalm often cited bears on it not at all. The critic who claims total silence overstates the case, and so does the defender who claims proof. The Quran is the witness that carries the weight.
dome-inscriptions: The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, built for the caliph Abd al-Malik and dated 691 to 692, carries some of the earliest dated Arabic quotations of the Quran. We give six things its inscriptions show. Within sixty years of the Prophet's death the text was fixed and familiar, quoted in public, adapted for a message and recognised by those who read it. The inscriptions leave some questions open, and the date of the first written copy is a matter for the manuscripts, which agree with them.
library-of-alexandria: A popular story says the caliph Umar ordered the Library of Alexandria burned in the 640s. We set out five facts. The story first appears six centuries after the conquest, in sources that cannot bear its weight, and it names a figure who died decades before the scene. The library declined over centuries through fire, war and neglect, and had almost certainly vanished before the Arabs arrived. Muslim and Western historians agree that the story is a legend.
jizya: Critics call the jizya a penalty for unbelief, and defenders call it a fee for protection and exemption from military service. We set out the facts from the Quran, the early legal manuals and later history. The jizya was a graduated annual tax on adult non-Muslim men, with real exemptions and real limits. It was tied to protection and military service and marked a difference of religion, and Muslims argued over how its payers should be treated. Each slogan keeps half of the record.
quran-preservation-reddit: A review of the scholarship on the Quran's preservation, posted to r/AcademicQuran in December 2025 and revised after comments from Marijn van Putten and others, weighs the arguments on both sides. We summarise its five main points. It supports the heart of the Muslim position: a standard text within two decades of the Prophet, followed by every later manuscript. It asks Muslims to drop claims the evidence does not bear, such as a Birmingham leaf from the Prophet's own day, and the case is stronger without them.
apostasy-in-islam: Critics say Islam punishes anyone who leaves it with death, and defenders cite the Quran on freedom of belief. We set out six facts, the hard ones first. Mainstream classical law prescribes death for apostasy on the strength of the hadith. The Quran condemns apostasy, places its punishment in the hereafter and says there is no compulsion in religion. Scholars today divide between those who keep the classical ruling and those who confine it to treason, among them a former Grand Mufti of Egypt.
before-you-convert-apostates-and-lgbt-fr: A social media list tells converts to hunt and shun people who leave Islam and to reject their LGBT friends. We answer in seven points. The Quran forbids spying on anyone's faith, and the Prophet forbade searching hearts. Classical law prescribed a penalty for apostasy after a call to repent, and some modern scholars hold that leaving is a matter between a person and God. No source tells a convert to hunt or discriminate. Islam forbids same-sex acts, does not count unacted desire as sin and prescribes no self-hatred.
crucifixion-quran: The crucifixion is where Islam and Christianity part most sharply, and the debate is three questions argued as one. We set out six facts on Quran 4:157. Historians and the Quran disagree on whether Jesus was crucified, and Muslims side with the Quran knowingly. The Quran denies that his enemies killed him and leaves the manner of his rescue largely unexplained, which the commentators tried to fill. The objection to atonement by proxy stands whatever happened, because the Hebrew prophets taught that each soul bears its own sin.
can-god-die: Charles Wesley's hymn asks how God could die for us, and a recent debate raised the question again. We give seven answers. The Hebrew Bible calls God everlasting and unchanging, and the New Testament calls Him the only one who has immortality. The church's formula that God died "in the flesh" either leaves the divine nature untouched, so that a man died, or makes God mortal. The idea that the innocent die so the guilty go free runs against Moses and Ezekiel. The Quran calls God the Living who does not die.
first-and-the-last: A social media argument says that because the Quran calls God "the First and the Last" (57:3) and Jesus uses the phrase in Revelation 1:17, the Quran affirms that Jesus is God. We give seven answers. Both books take the title from Isaiah, where it belongs to the God beside whom there is no other. The Prophet's own prayer and the commentators explain it in the Quran. In Revelation the speaker says "I died", calls on "my God" and receives his revelation from God. A shared phrase is no shared belief.
islam-arian-heresy-claim: A social media post says Islam is an Arian Christian heresy that councils refuted in 325, 431 and 525 and that John of Damascus refuted in 649. We give seven answers. The post's labels contradict one another, and of its four dates two are real, one has no council and one is wrong by a century. The councils were votes, one overturned within a generation. John offered the Arian charge as a guess, and his own summary of Muslim belief, a God neither begotten nor begetting, contradicts it.
six-articles-of-faith: The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) listed six articles of faith when Gabriel asked him what iman is. We explain each one: belief in God, the angels, the books, the messengers, the Last Day and the decree. The first names who God is, the next three describe how He speaks to people, the fifth says where the story ends and the sixth that nothing escapes His knowledge. Each rests on the Quran and the hadith of Gabriel, and the theological schools agree on the list.
fate-and-free-will: If God knows what you will do, how is it your choice? Belief in qadar, the decree, is one of the six articles of faith. We answer seven questions from the sources. The Quran addresses its readers as agents who can believe or disbelieve, and says in the same breath that nothing happens outside God's will. Muslim scholars disagreed on how the two fit, and the schools that resolved the tension in either direction lost to the middle position. The practical teaching is clear: act, and trust God with the result.
sadness-and-depression-in-islam: Some young Muslims are told that feeling empty or depressed is forbidden. We test that claim against the sources in seven points. Five are firm: the Quran records a prophet's grief, Mary, Job and Jonah voiced distress without rebuke, the Prophet (peace be upon him) wept at his son's death and called it mercy, he sought refuge from worry and grief, and his sayings command treatment. The claim fails. The tradition asks no one to hide pain, and gives the sufferer prayer, company and care.
end-of-time: Popular writing on Islamic end times mixes the Quran, the hadith and later tradition. We place five beliefs in their layer. That the Hour will come, at a time no creature knows, rests on the Quran. The signs, the Dajjal and the return of Jesus rest on widely transmitted hadith. The Mahdi and the order of events rest on reports scholars weigh differently, and Muslims may differ there. Anyone who offers a date, or names a living person as the Dajjal or the Mahdi, claims more than the sources give.
blasphemy-and-insults-to-the-prophet: Each controversy over a cartoon or a burned Quran brings the charge that Islam punishes criticism with death. We separate four layers: scripture, classical law, modern statute and street violence. The Quran tells Muslims to expect mockery and meet it with patience, and the Prophet bore insults and refused to have the insulters killed. Classical jurists treated insult to the Prophet as grave and disagreed sharply on the penalty. All placed the matter with a court. Mob violence has no warrant in any layer.
sharia-and-hudud: In a newsroom sharia means punishment, and in a mosque it means a way of life. We answer five myths. Sharia is a path, and its rulings are the work of jurists who disagreed openly. The hudud are a small part of that work, surrounded by strict proof requirements, the rule of doubt and the advice to avert them, and repentance is written into the verses. The classical schools upheld the fixed punishments, and modern scholars differ on some, such as apostasy.
quranic-ethics: The Quran puts the command to pray beside the command to feed the poor. We set out seven of its most repeated ethical commands, each with its text, its classical reading and the place it is hardest to keep. Each protects someone weak at the moment of testing: a party to a dispute, a neighbour, an aged parent, a person relying on a promise, someone absent from a conversation, a citizen before an official and an orphan. None can be enforced by a court in every case, so each depends on conscience before God.
why-no-interest: Interest is the one commercial practice the Quran threatens with war (2:279). We give five reasons the sources and scholars give for the ban. The Quran forbids riba in language it uses for nothing else in trade, and the Prophet repeated the ban in his last public address. The reasoning holds that a loan is help, that profit should follow risk, and that compounding debt falls hardest on the weak. Scholars still disagree on how the rule applies to modern banking and how far Islamic finance has met it.
women-in-the-prophets-life: The early sources are full of women who advise, narrate, teach, fund and decide. We introduce seven in the life of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), in the order they enter it. Khadija believed first, Umm Salama gave advice that ended a crisis, Aisha taught the Companions and Hafsa kept the sheets of the Quran. The sources were compiled by men, focus on women close to the Prophet and say little of ordinary women, and they still record these women's names, words and decisions with frankness.
companions-who-started-with-nothing: Quraysh prized rank and lineage, and many of the first Muslims had neither. We tell the stories of six Companions who came from slavery, a foreign land, a robber tribe and poverty, and went on to shape the community. The torture of Bilal and the family of Yasir, the arrival of Abdul Rahman in Medina and Abu Hurayra's attendance on the Prophet are well attested, and some reports on Salman and Abu Dharr rest on weaker chains. Their lives answer the idea that Islam was a movement of the powerful.
questions-about-aisha: Aisha bint Abu Bakr is the wife of the Prophet (peace be upon him) about whom most questions are asked, and most come from one report. We answer five of them from the sources. The best-attested report puts the marriage at six and its consummation at nine, and scholars through the centuries accepted it, while a minority of modern scholars argue for a later age. Neither view treats the practice as a model for today. Most of her record concerns her work as a jurist and teacher.
child-marriage-in-islam: Child marriage is a real problem in parts of the world, and it is often defended with religion. We set out five facts from the sources, kept apart from custom. The Quran sets no age and ties marriage to maturity, sound judgement and a solemn covenant. The Prophet made the bride's consent a condition. The classical jurists disagreed about marriage before maturity, and none allowed consummation before a girl was able. Scholars read the reports about Aisha as a particular case, and Muslim states legislate marriage ages.
does-the-quran-allow-wife-beating: Quran 4:34 is the verse most often quoted against Islam on women. We read it in five points. In full, it ties the husband's role to his duty to provide, orders the steps from advice to withdrawal and only then a limited act, ends them when the problem ends, and sends a lasting rift to arbitration. The Prophet (peace be upon him) never struck a woman and praised restraint, and the jurists forbade any blow that injures. Read with those limits, the verse restrains a husband far more than critics allow.
a-father-says-this-is-islam: Some who leave Islam describe a father who enforced every rule with the words "this is Islam". We believe accounts of harm, and ask a narrower question: are the rules in the sources? Of seven rules, three are plainly forbidden by the sources: striking a wife in anger, forcing a daughter into marriage and mocking a family member. Two are customs with a seed of duty, where the sources give kindness and modesty. One is mixed. One is false: that hatred of a people is part of the faith.
slavery-in-islam: Slavery was universal in the world the Quran addressed. We set out six facts on what the Islamic sources did with it. They closed most routes into slavery, opened many routes out, and attached rights and reward to treating slaves well. They also left the institution standing and regulated concubinage and sale, and Muslim societies kept and traded slaves for centuries, sometimes harshly. The Quran and the Prophet moved the law towards freedom, and the record of later societies should be judged by that direction.
homosexuality-in-islam: Islamic teaching on homosexuality is traditional and plain, and the treatment of people has often fallen short of it. We set out five facts. The sources and the classical consensus forbid same-sex acts, and the revisionist readings of Lot's story found no support in the classical schools. The Quran fixes no penalty, and the hadith used for death is disputed. The tradition distinguishes inclination from act, sets strict rules of proof and privacy, and discourages exposing what God has concealed. The prohibition and its limits both stand.
hijab-and-modesty: The headscarf is the most argued-over symbol of Muslim life. We set out five facts from the two Quranic verses on dress, the hadith on how the first generation read them, and the views of the jurists. The command of modesty addresses men and women. The first generation and the classical jurists read the instruction to cover the head and chest as binding, and they disagreed about the face and hands. The law fixes no worldly penalty, and the act is meant to be freely chosen.
before-you-convert-women-and-marriage: A social media list tells converts to treat women as inferior, says women converts must be circumcised and accept being a "minor wife", and demands near-total covering for women only. We give seven answers. The Quran measures every person by righteousness and promises men and women the same reward. The husband's charge in 4:34 is tied to his duty to provide. Female circumcision rests on a report its own compiler called weak, and Egypt's Dar al-Ifta has declared it forbidden. Polygyny is bounded by justice, and modesty binds men too.
houris-and-paradise: The "72 virgins" has become a joke and a slander. We set out five facts. The Quran names the hur 'in and gives no number. The seventy-two comes from one disputed report about the martyr, and no doctrine can rest on it. The Quran promises Paradise to men and women on equal terms, describes it in images scholars read as pointers to what cannot be described, and places God's approval above them all. The popular picture of a reward for violence has no basis in the Quran, the hadith or the schools.
war-and-killing-in-islam: Critics quote the Quran's verses on fighting without their setting. We set out five facts. The first permission to fight came after years of persecution in Mecca. The texts carry limits the Prophet and his successors spelled out: no killing of women, children, the old or clergy, no mutilation, no destruction of crops and no breaking of treaties. The Quran's verse on the value of a single life frames the verses on fighting. The classical jurists did permit state wars beyond defence, and Muslim history includes violence the sources condemn.
quran-science-claims-graded: The Quran describes the natural world in many verses. We set out four of the strongest cases, each in the verse's own words: the water cycle, the orbits of the heavenly bodies, the stages of the embryo and the speech of the ant. Each is described correctly in seventh-century Arabic, and nothing in them has been overturned. Al Faruqi held that the Quran's miracle is its language, and Ibn Rushd advised reading scripture in harmony with demonstrated knowledge. Read without stretching, the verses stand.
natural-world-verses: The Quran treats nature as a sign, aya, the same word it uses for its verses. We read five verses on the natural world, each with its classical and its modern reading. Believers who find modern science in a verse must set aside the classical readings, which did not see it there. Critics who find errors must read a poetic image as a technical claim, which the first hearers did not. The search for science in the Quran grew after Maurice Bucaille's book of 1976, and Muslim scholars have criticised it.
quranic-stories-and-history: The Quran retells the past as a lesson and rarely gives dates or maps. We compare six of its stories with inscriptions, archaeology and neighbouring traditions. Abraha's Yemeni inscriptions, Nineveh and the Tamudi of an Assyrian text match closely. 'Ad has no secure archaeological match, and the Sleepers and Dhu al-Qarnayn share their outline with older legends. None has been shown false. A text that means to teach needs no site plan, and the Quran says it relates these stories as lessons.
prophets-you-may-not-know: The Quran names twenty-five prophets and says there were others, for "there is no community to which a warner has not come". We introduce five who appear only briefly, with what the Quran says, what the commentators added and where they disagree. The text says little about Idris, Dhul-Kifl and the others, and the commentators' identifications are informed guesses that no Muslim is required to believe. The Prophet's guidance on reports from the People of the Book applies: neither believe nor deny them.
quran-mysteries-in-the-stories: Some Quranic stories leave out names, places and dates, and the commentators filled them in with different answers. We take five such puzzles, among them the servant whose knowledge exceeds a prophet's, the barrier that stands until God decides, the number of the Sleepers and the people of the well. In each, the Quran states what the believer needs and withholds the rest. The reports that fill the gaps differ, and many are weak. Where the Quran gives detail, the detail serves the lesson.
gods-attributes-and-anthropomorphism: Critics say the Quran's verses on God's hand, face and rising describe a God with a body. We set out seven points from the classical texts. The early scholars affirmed what the text says, refused any likeness to creation, and then differed over whether to interpret the words. The Quran answers its most human image in a single verse: "Nothing is like unto Him" (42:11). The Bible uses the same kind of language. The record gives no support to the charge that early Muslims pictured God as a body.
temporary-marriage-mutah: Mutah is a fixed-term marriage contract, and Muslims disagree about it more sharply than about almost any other question of family law. We set out seven points from the sources. They show a permission given briefly to men on campaign, then a prohibition, with the last statement placed at the conquest of Mecca. The contrary reading of 4:24 depends on a variant the recited text lacks. The critic's charge that Islam permits prostitution under another name fails on either side of the Muslim debate.
do-muslims-worship-muhammad: Critics say Muslims make Muhammad (peace be upon him) a second object of devotion, pointing to the blessings, the poems and the open love Muslims show him. We give seven points. The Quran calls him a servant, he rejected exaggerated praise, and Abu Bakr answered the charge on the day of his death: whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad is dead. Blessing him follows a command of the Quran, and treating him as divine breaks it. Muslims give him love, obedience and imitation.
crusades-facts: The Crusades are retold on both sides as a clash with a clear villain. We set out six facts documented in Latin, Greek and Arabic sources. The Crusaders came at a Christian emperor's request and conquered more than he asked. They massacred Jerusalem in 1099, and Saladin's recapture in 1187 came on better terms. Muslim rulers fought one another as readily as Christian princes did, and the unity later claimed on each side did not exist. The record excuses no massacre on either side.
muslims-by-the-numbers: Public talk about Muslims and the West runs on guesses. We set out seven figures from the Pew Research Center count published in June 2025, which covers 2010 to 2020, with the limits of each. The count describes a religion of about two billion people, centred in Asia, growing mainly through births, and forming about six per cent of Europe. Projections for the West depend on assumptions about migration and fertility, so any figure quoted should name who counted it and for which year.
islam-in-china: China has more than twenty million Muslims and a Muslim presence that reaches back to the century after the Prophet (peace be upon him). We set out five facts. Muslims arrived within the first Islamic century, settled and intermarried, and became the Hui, who built mosques in local style, wrote theology in classical Chinese and produced an admiral and a sultan. The history also includes nineteenth-century massacres and uprisings, and severe restrictions in more than one era, most recently in Xinjiang.
kharijites-and-takfir: Extremist groups declare other Muslims unbelievers so that they can kill them, a practice called takfir. We set out six facts on its origin. The first takfiris were pious men in Ali's army who rebelled over a political decision, branded the Prophet's family unbelievers and killed Ali at prayer. The Prophet (peace be upon him) had described their type in advance. The mainstream answered with a settled rule: no Muslim is declared an unbeliever for a sin, and the question belongs to qualified judges after proof.
taqiyya-myths: Taqiyya is cited online as proof that Muslims may lie to non-Muslims at will. We answer five myths from the Quran and hadith. The Quran allows a believer under compulsion to protect his life by what he says, while his heart stays firm in faith (16:106). The Prophet (peace be upon him) allowed the tortured their words, kept treaties against his own advantage and condemned lying as a mark of the hypocrite. The permissions in war and reconciliation are narrow. No text permits lying to non-Muslims at will.
before-your-first-friday-prayer: Friday noon is the weekly gathering of the Muslim community, and visitors are welcome. We set out seven things a first-time visitor should know, in the order of the day: the call, the washing, the dress and the hall, the sermon, the prayer and what follows. Take off your shoes, dress modestly, sit quietly through the sermon and watch the rows form. A visitor need not wash, bow or recite. Each part of the service has a reason in the Quran or the hadith.
hajj-rites-explained: Ismail al Faruqi defined the hajj as the fifth pillar of Islam, made up of intention, ihram, circling the Kaaba, the standing, sacrifice and stoning. We explain six rites, each with the text or report behind it and its meaning. Every rite has a source in the Quran or the Prophet's own pilgrimage, and the tradition explains each by the memory of Abraham, Hagar and Ishmael. The schools differ on details, such as the walk between the hills and the timing of the standing.
ramadan-last-ten-nights: The last ten nights of Ramadan hold the night the Quran calls better than a thousand months. We set out five things to know. The Prophet (peace be upon him) narrowed the search to the odd nights and declined to name one, so the sources leave the date open. The twenty-seventh has Companion opinion behind it, and no text makes it certain. The practice is fixed: wake the household, give more, pray, ask for pardon and, for those who can, keep the retreat of i'tikaf.
funeral-dhikr-dua: Much of Muslim devotion outside the daily prayers is dhikr, du'a and the funeral rites, and Ismail al Faruqi noted that English "prayer" fits only du'a. We describe six practices in the order a believer meets them: two of the heart and tongue, and four of the funeral. They rest on a few Quranic verses and on reports in al-Bukhari and Muslim of how the Prophet washed, shrouded, prayed over and buried the dead. The schools agree where the sources are explicit and differ where they are silent.
scholars-who-shaped-islamic-study: Most of what a student reads in a Muslim school was shaped by a few people. We introduce seven, in order of period. Ibn Abbas set how the Quran was explained, Ibn Ishaq gave the Prophet's life its shape and Abu Dawud sorted the reports that law rests on. Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a Christian, and al-Kindi opened the Greek sciences to Arabic readers, and al-Ash'ari and al-Ghazali set the terms of theology. The same habit recurs: a text, a chain, a check and a reply.
western-scholars-of-islam: Muslims have long read Western scholars of Islam with a mix of use and objection. We introduce five, in order of birth: Geiger, Caetani, Jeffery, Goitein and Karen Armstrong, with where Muslim scholars answer each. Caetani and Jeffery gathered material in one place, and Goitein supplied documents no polemic can easily dismiss. Geiger and Armstrong show how much an outsider's answer depends on the question asked. The disagreement is mostly about premises: a scholar who assumes a human Quran reads parallels as borrowings.
islamic-art-and-the-one-god: Mosques show no pictures of God and walls of pattern that seem to run past their edges. The common explanation is that Islam forbids images. We set out five ideas from Ismail al Faruqi's account, in which the pattern states a belief: God is beyond every likeness. That belief produces stylised plants, geometric figures, endless pattern and the written word. His sources say what he says they say, and the monuments show the habits he describes. Borrowed forms and royal taste shaped Islamic art as well.
mosques-adapt-to-place: A mosque needs a clean place for prayer facing Mecca, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) said the whole earth was made a place of prayer for him. We describe five mosques, from a courtyard of mud brick to timber and tile, that show architecture adapting to place. Islam fixes the essentials: a clean ground, the direction of the Kaaba and prayer to God alone. Within those limits Muslims built with whatever was at hand, and the classical warnings against ostentation still apply.
islamophobia-facts: The word Islamophobia names real suffering for some and serves to end arguments for others. We set out five facts on where the word came from and what it covers. Hostility to Muslims is old and is recorded in killings, assaults and police statistics, and it falls on people who are themselves the largest group of victims of extremist violence. The word is recent and its dispute is fair. Criticism of Islam as a set of ideas is open to anyone, and contempt for a person is another thing.
islamisation-of-the-west: The claim of an "Islamisation of the West" turns migration, courts, advocacy groups and mosques into the parts of a plan. We examine six pieces of the claim on their own record. Dearborn is under no Sharia law, and the story was satire taken for news. The building near Ground Zero was a community centre two blocks away. The listing of CAIR was made public in breach of due process, a serious and disputed episode. Each piece turns out smaller and more ordinary than the claim needs.
muslim-societies-backwardness-claim: A common argument reads the lower development scores of Muslim-majority countries as a verdict on Islam. We set out five facts. The numbers are often real, and Arab researchers were the first to publish them in detail. The single-cause story fails against the data. Oil wealth predicts authoritarian government in Muslim and non-Muslim states alike, colonial institutions gave some states a harder start, and the category spans countries from the United Arab Emirates, fifteenth in the world on human development, to some of the poorest.
black-stone-and-kissing: Critics say Muslims kiss a black rock, an idol left over from pagan Arabia. We give five facts. The Black Stone is a marker set in the Kaaba, damaged and reframed over the centuries. Muslims touch or kiss it because the Prophet (peace be upon him) did, and Umar said he knew it had no power of its own. The rite is optional, and the pilgrim's prayer goes to God. The same test clears Jews at the Western Wall and Christians at the Stone of Anointing.
women-in-islamic-law-testimony-inheritan: Complaints about Islam and women bundle testimony, inheritance, polygamy, honour killing, genital cutting and a husband's claim on his wife. We take six points in turn. The rules on testimony, inheritance and polygamy are in the Quran, each with a stated purpose and limit: forgetting in loans, the duty of support, and justice among wives. Honour killing and female genital cutting have no sound basis in the texts, and the Prophet refused a husband the right to kill. The hadith on intimacy is moral counsel.
fly-hadith-and-adult-suckling: Two sound hadith appear in lists of "strange teachings": the fly that falls into a drink and the woman told to nurse a grown man. We give five points. Both reports are authentic. The fly report is a household instruction, and scholars from Ibn Khaldun to Shah Wali Allah set such instructions apart from the law. The report about Sahla records one ruling for a household left in difficulty by the end of adoption, which the Prophet's wives argued over and most jurists confined to her case.
camel-urine-hadith: A common reply online says Muslims are told to drink camel urine. The claim rests on a real report in al-Bukhari and Muslim, so we answer it in five points. The report records a remedy given to a group of sick men on one occasion, and the same narration goes on to describe a murder, a robbery and a punishment. No school of law makes the practice a duty or a recommended act, and the schools differ only on purity and medicinal use.
quran-grammar-errors-claim: Critics say the Quran contains grammatical mistakes and so fails its own challenge. We set out four facts. The argument rests on a few verses, chiefly 4:162, 5:69 and 20:63, and two early reports, one attributed to A'isha. The classical scholars examined every case from the sources the critics now cite. The constructions are attested in Arabic speech and poetry. The variant readings show that the teachers of the Quran knew the regular forms and kept what they had received. The reports about scribes concern spelling.
quran-challenge-met-claim: A social media post says al-Ma'arri's al-Fusul wa al-Ghayat and the Christian True Furqan have met the Quran's challenge to produce a surah like it (2:23). We give seven answers. Al-Ma'arri's book is an exhortation in praise of God, and one modern study holds he never meant it as a rival, while Nicholson reports that its author judged it inferior. The True Furqan is a missionary pastiche of 1999 built from the Quran's own vocabulary. Those who know the language have received neither as the Quran's equal.
quran-pronoun-shifts-iltifat: Readers of the Quran in translation meet sudden shifts between He, We and I, and critics take them as signs of a careless or composite text. We give six answers. The device, iltifat, was used by poets before Islam, and the rhetoricians named, classified and explained it. The Quran uses it far more than any poet. Abdel Haleem's counts show the turns fall where the meaning turns, and Robinson's survey shows they mark God's majesty and His oneness and keep the Messenger outside the speech.
who-wrote-the-quran: Critics ask who wrote the Quran and whether anyone can show it. We give six answers. On the Muslim account the Quran has a named author, and on every account a named recipient. The text records the charge that a man or helpers produced it and answers with a challenge. Tradition and critical scholarship agree that an early, fairly stable text existed soon after the Prophet's death. The evidence cannot decide between revelation and human composition, and that choice rests on how a reader weighs the challenge and the Prophet's character.
quran-contradictions-claims: Online lists of "contradictions" in the Quran run to dozens of entries and rest on a few patterns: numbers that seem not to add up, time spans that seem to clash and acts given to more than one agent. We answer six cases. The days of creation add up once the Arabic is read as Arabic. The days of a thousand and fifty thousand years measure different things. The taking of souls is ascribed to God and His angels as Badr's throw is to God and the Prophet. Several answers go back to Ibn Abbas.
preservation-and-truth: Critics say a perfectly preserved text is still false if its content is false, and as logic the objection has force. We give five answers. Preservation shows that the Quran we read is the Quran the early Muslims recited, and on its own it shows no more. For Muslims it supports one premise, that the text is the unaltered word of God. The case for the rest rests on the content, the character of the Prophet (peace be upon him) and the arguments for God, each open to weighing.
relationship-with-god: A sincere Christian reply says that its proof of Christ is a personal relationship with God, and implies that Islam offers submission without one. We give five answers. The Quran and the hadith describe a God who is near, who answers, who loves and who forgives directly, and Muslims speak of that bond in the vocabulary of mercy, nearness and servanthood. A personal testimony deserves respect, and it cannot settle which tradition is true, for the Christian or for the Muslim. The revelation itself must decide.
buraq-and-miracle-stories: Critics call Islam a fairy tale, citing a winged steed that carried a man to heaven and a talking donkey. We set out six stories and what the sources say. The Quran presents the Night Journey as a sign and names no steed. The hadith describe the Buraq as a white animal between a donkey and a mule in size, and the wings and human face come from later pictures. The talking donkey is a fabricated report that Muslim critics rejected. A sceptic of miracles must apply the same test to the Bible.
raids-badr-and-the-conquest-of-mecca: One critique counts 75 raids led by Muhammad (peace be upon him) and calls him the aggressor in nearly all. We set out six facts. The sources record caravan raids, a killing at Nakhla, two executions after Badr, exceptions to the amnesty at Mecca and gifts to former enemies. They also record that Quraysh expelled the believers and marched on Medina, that the Prophet disowned Khalid's killings, and that amnesty and the release of captives were the larger pattern.
revisionist-case-weighed: A revisionist school holds that the first century of Islam is a gap and that the Quran and sunna took shape in the eighth and ninth centuries. We give six answers. The school is right that the seventh century is thinly documented. The record is far from empty: two manuscripts date within about forty years of 632, coins and a dated monument name Muhammad (peace be upon him) within sixty, a papyrus counts years from the hijra by 643, and Christian writers of that century mention a prophet among the Arabs.
kaab-ibn-al-ashraf-and-the-poets: Critics say Muhammad (peace be upon him) had his critics killed at night, naming Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Abu Rafi' and the poets Asma bint Marwan and Abu Afak. We give four answers. Two killings are in Sahih al-Bukhari, and both belong to a war for Medina's survival: Ka'b went to Mecca after Badr to raise Quraysh, and Abu Rafi' helped raise the army that besieged Medina. The two poets' stories fail: one comes through a narrator named as its forger, and the other has no chain that holds.
medina-jewish-tribes-and-qurayza: Critics cite Qaynuqa, Nadir, Qurayza and Khaybar to argue that the Prophet (peace be upon him) answered the Jews of Medina with violence, and one compares Qurayza to genocide. We set out six facts. The four episodes ended differently: two expulsions, one execution of fighting men and one settlement in which the people kept their land. The Qurayza verdict is hard, and the record shows a wartime charge, an arbitrator from the tribe's own allies and a death toll the early scholars did not fix.
first-revelation-demonic-claim: A critique says the first revelation was a demonic visitation that left the Prophet (peace be upon him) fearing possession. We give seven answers. The sources record his fear at Hira, a report of grief and the Meccan charges of madness and sorcery. They also record who answered the fear and how: Khadija, Waraqa and a test. The Quran describes Gabriel early, names him later and states the devil theory only to deny it. The accounts give no support to a demonic origin.
islamic-rites-before-islam: Critics say Islam's rites were already old and were taken from the pagans of Mecca or the Jews. We give six answers. The Muslim sources record much of this openly: Mecca was modest, Quraysh rebuilt the Kaaba with Muhammad (peace be upon him) present, and Quraysh and the Jews of Medina fasted Ashura. The charge of concealment fails because the record is open. The Quran is specific about what it removed, such as the pagan practice of circling the Kaaba naked.
terrorism-and-muslims-the-data: Critics say terrorism is Islamic at root and that most of it is committed by Muslims. We set out seven facts on the figures and the texts. Jihadist groups have killed thousands, many in Muslim-majority countries, and some attackers cite scripture. The figures of 85 per cent, 4 per cent and twenty times have no named source, and the main databases tell a different story. The texts attackers cite carry limits that the tradition applied from its earliest years.
magic-jinn-and-satan-hadiths: Critics cite hadith about magic, Satan and the jinn as proof that the Prophet (peace be upon him) shared the superstitions of his age. We take six reports. The report of the spell is sound by chain, and most scholars accept it, and it describes a temporary bodily affliction with no change to the message. The sayings about Satan are sound and open to figurative reading. The jinn reports concern the unseen, which readers accept or decline by belief. The argument is about meaning, and a fair critic must argue it there.
sira-ibn-ishaq-hisham-tabari: A critique says the early biographies of the Prophet (peace be upon him) are a poor foundation: Ibn Ishaq's book is lost, Ibn Hisham trimmed it and al-Tabari wrote three centuries later. We set out five facts. The biographies are late, edited and sometimes incomplete, and the critique is accurate on that. They are no single block to accept or reject whole. Muslim scholars grade the reports and compare the authors, and the Quran rests on a transmission of its own.
prophets-marriages-zaynab-and-others: Critics point to Zaynab bint Jahsh, to captive wives such as Safiyya and to 33:50, and conclude that desire ruled the Prophet's household. We set out seven facts. The sources record the verse on Zaynab, the captives taken in war and the Prophet's privilege, and the Quran names the embarrassment itself in 33:37. They give no support to the charge of incest, since 4:23 excludes adopted sons, or to the romance story later commentators rejected. They give tribal, diplomatic and social reasons for most of the marriages.
apes-and-pigs-and-the-jews: Critics say the Prophet (peace be upon him) was hostile to Jews as a people, citing the verses on apes and pigs and a hadith about killing Jews. We set out six facts. The Quran criticises named Jewish groups for specific acts. The apes and pigs verses describe a past punishment, and neither classical reading names Jews of today. The phrase quoted as "kill every Jew" is spoken by Byzantine courtiers. The Quran praises upright Jews, and the Prophet's dealings with Jews included trade, treaties and justice.
satanic-verses-report: An early story says the Prophet (peace be upon him) once recited words praising three Meccan goddesses and withdrew them as Satan's. We set out five facts. Early books record the story, and as a hadith it lacks a sound connected chain, the standard collections omit it, and scholars from Qadi Iyad to al-Albani rejected it. Sura 53 reads as a continuous attack on the idols, and 22:52 can be read without the story. Ibn Hajar and Watt gave it more weight, and that disagreement is honest.
abrogation-and-the-sword-verse: Critics say the doctrine of abrogation lets the Sword Verse, 9:5, cancel the Quran's verses on peace, including 2:256 and 5:69. We set out five facts. Abrogation is a real classical doctrine, 9:5 does command fighting, and some early commentators said it overrode gentler verses. The doctrine covers legal rulings under strict conditions, scholars counted the abrogated verses from none to over a hundred, and many read 2:256 and 5:69 as standing. Verse 9:5 itself sits among verses on treaties and asylum.
end-of-the-world-prediction: A critique says the Prophet (peace be upon him) predicted the end of the world 500 years after his call, in 1110, and so was a false prophet. We set out five facts. The report is real and contains the number 500. It expresses a hope that the community would last at least half a day and names no starting point. The Quran and the hadith of Gabriel place the time of the Hour with God alone. Al-Tabari read the report as a countdown, which was one scholar's calculation.
race-in-quran-and-hadith: Critics say the Quran and the hadith teach contempt for black people, citing a curse on Noah's descendants and a few harsh reports. We give five answers. The Quran ranks people by righteousness and names no curse on any race, and the farewell sermon says so plainly. The lives of Bilal, Usama, Salman and the Negus show a community that honoured people of every origin. Several quoted reports are weak, drawn from Israelite sources or misread. Some medieval writers held the prejudices of their age, and the sources judge them.
quran-on-christians: Critics say the Quran singles out Christians: it calls their belief disbelief, forbids friendship with them and demands a tax, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) cursed them and marched against them. We give seven answers. The Quran denies that Jesus is God and calls the Trinity a mistake, and 9:29 and the deathbed words are firm texts. Each has a context: a belief, an alliance, a war, a practice at graves. Weighed together, the verses dispute Christian doctrine and honour Christian people.
fighting-verses-in-context: Nine passages are quoted to show that the Quran commands war on unbelievers as such, among them 9:5, 9:29, 8:12 and 2:191. We set out six facts, with the setting the classical commentators give for each. Each passage was spoken in a war and sits beside verses that limit it: treaties honoured, asylum granted, captives released and fighting stopped when the enemy stops. The language is martial and 5:33 is severe. The commentators and jurists did not read these verses as a standing order to kill unbelievers.
first-muslims-kept-the-faith: A critique says Islam began as a money-making scheme that failed in Mecca and succeeded only by the sword in Medina. We test it against the thirteen Meccan years in five points. The Prophet (peace be upon him) was offered wealth and refused it. His wife and a cousin met the first revelation with fear and reassurance, with no sign of design. A small community grew steadily and endured blows, boycott and exile, and some fled to Abyssinia. The sword played no part in that period.
quran-anachronism-claims: Critics list supposed historical slips in the Quran: a king who argued with Abraham, Saul in the age of Moses, Job made a descendant of Abraham, crucifixion in Pharaoh's court and prophets called Muslims. We test seven claims against the verses. Nimrod is a commentator's name, Talut stands after Moses in the verse, Job's place in 6:84 turns on a pronoun, and 20:71 describes hanging on a trunk. The word Muslim is used in its root sense. Two questions remain open, and the claims shrink.
jihad-meaning-quran-hadith-jurists: Critics say jihad always means fighting, outranks the five pillars and makes the hadith lists of pillars contradict one another. We set out five facts. Jihad means effort, and in the Medinan verses and the law books it often means fighting, which critics read correctly. The claim that it always means fighting fails against the Meccan verses, the reports that rank other deeds first and the jurists' treatment of fighting as a limited, collective duty. The popular "greater jihad" saying is weak.
talmud-midrash-apocrypha-borrowing: Critics say the Quran copied Jewish and Christian writings, listing Cain and the raven, Abraham and the idols, the queen of Sheba and the clay birds of the child Jesus. We give six answers. Some parallels are close and old, such as the saying behind 5:32, and others rest on sources later than the Quran. No parallel proves copying, since stories moved by speech and a common stock of lore lies behind both. The Quran says openly that it confirms earlier scripture.
quran-iblis-fallen-angels-borrowing: In 1926 Rabbi Leo Jung argued that the Quran took its stories of the angels, Iblis and Harut and Marut from Jewish and Christian informants. We give seven answers. Jung showed that the three traditions told similar stories about the angels, Adam and the devil, and his parallels are worth knowing. His conclusion goes further than his evidence. He mixes the Quran with later Muslim legend that Muslim critics had set aside, and his link to Augustine does not hold.
iblis-and-the-command-to-prostrate: A Christian polemic argues that Iblis, being of the jinn (18:50), was never commanded to bow to Adam, so God punished him unjustly. We give eight answers. The Quran says the reverse in God's own words, "when I commanded you" (7:12), and Iblis admits it. The commentators explain that he stood among the angels and was addressed with them. The prostration honoured Adam in obedience to God, as the bowing of Joseph's family shows. Iblis's plea that God put him in error is the excuse of the one who refused.
i-read-the-entire-quran-reply: In May 2026 A. C. Rosenthal published a widely shared essay saying he read the whole Quran, the hadith and the Sira and found reasons to reject Islam. We give seven answers. The essay is honest about his Muslim friend. Several of its statements about the sources are wrong: al-Suyuti shortened the lists of abrogated verses, Ibn Ishaq was no Companion, the poets' killings rest on rejected reports and 2:191 is bounded by 2:190. Its two central arguments rest on premises the sources do not support.
is-yahweh-satan: Online debates ask whether Yahweh, the God of the Hebrew Bible, is really Satan, citing passages where He incites a king, sends a lying spirit, tests Job and commands wars of destruction. We set out seven such passages and answer each. They show a tradition wrestling with evil under one God, first by ascribing everything to Him and later by naming agents who act within His permission. For a Muslim reader the Quran's instruction is plain: "our God and your God is one" (29:46). Iblis is a creature, and never God.
who-was-yahweh-archaeological-origins: Excavation has added a second source to the Bible's account of where Yahweh worship began. We set out seven discoveries from Egypt, Sinai, Judah and Moab. They show a god associated with the south, worshipped in regional forms, sometimes paired with an asherah, served at royal shrines that later reformers closed and spoken of in the terms used for neighbouring national gods. Archaeology makes the early history richer and more complicated. It cannot show who Yahweh is, and it gives no support to the claim that he is Satan.
was-yahweh-one-of-many-gods: The Hebrew Bible is the founding text of monotheism, and it also speaks of a council of gods and sons of God allotted the nations. We set out seven clues from ancient Israelite religion: the name El beside Yahweh, a divine council in the vocabulary of Ugarit, Deuteronomy 32:8 and a psalm in which the gods are judged. The Bible's language moves from God's incomparability among the gods to the denial that any other god exists. The evidence leaves open how that movement should be understood.
early-christians-yahweh-evil-gnosticism-: Modern writers cite Marcion and the Gnostics as proof that the earliest Christians knew Yahweh to be evil, or Satan. We set out seven points. Marcion and the teachers later called Gnostics held that the creator was lower than the highest God, and some portrayed him harshly. Their opponents defended one God of creation and redemption, and most of the church followed. The claim that early Christians knew Yahweh as Satan has little support: the nearest parallels are the name Samael in one myth and the medieval Bogomils.
is-yahweh-the-same-as-allah: The Quran never uses the name Yahweh, the Hebrew Bible never uses Allah, and some conclude that they name different gods. We answer seven questions. Yahweh is the Bible's name for the God of Abraham and Moses, and Allah is the Arabic word the Quran uses for the same God, who speaks to Moses at the bush. Islam disputes much of what the earlier scriptures now say about Him and the Christian account of Jesus. It rejects absolutely the claim that the God of Moses is Satan.
hanif-poets-and-musaylima: A critique says the Quran took its content and style from the Hanif poets Zayd ibn Amr and Waraqa ibn Nawfal and from Musaylima, quoting Zayd word for word. We test it in five points. Arabia did hold men who rejected idols, and the Islamic sources say so. Zayd died before the revelation began, Waraqa appears only as a witness, no passage of the Quran matches a line of either, and Musaylima appeared late in the Prophet's life. The claim of word-for-word copying needs the verses, and none is given.
schacht-isnads-dating-hadith: Joseph Schacht argued that the chains of transmission for hadith grew backwards over time, and critics repeat his conclusion in strong forms. We give eight answers. Schacht and his followers were right that hadith were forged, and Muslim scholars said so long before them. The evidence goes against them on late writing, on untested chains and on what their figures measure. The dating of particular reports remains a live debate among Muslim and Western scholars. Each report should be examined on its merits, as the classical critics did.
was-muhammad-illiterate-ummi: Critics say the Quran calls Muhammad (peace be upon him) unlettered and then opens its first revelation with "Read", and that it says man was made from clots. We give five answers. Ummi can mean unlettered or a member of a people without a scripture, and 62:2 favours the second. Verse 29:48 concerns books before the revelation and was addressed to people who knew him. "Read" is best taken as "recite", and 'alaq has a range wider than "clot". The reports of his writing are disputed.
ridda-wars-abu-bakr-fadak: A critique says Abu Bakr's Ridda wars were fought over unpaid zakah and that Fatima's claim to Fadak was refused for gain. We set out five facts. Zakah stood at the centre of the first dispute, and Fatima's request was refused, as the critique says. The Ridda wars were also about rival prophets, tribal secession and a public duty, and Umar tested the decision and then agreed. On Fadak, Sunni and Shia sources give different accounts of the same event, and each side holds its position with reasons.
nabi-and-rasul: Critics say the Quran's two words for prophet, nabi and rasul, show confusion, and that scholars invented a distinction the text lacks. We give six answers. In 22:52 the Quran lists the two as separate, and calls Moses and Ishmael both. The classical scholars agreed that every messenger is a prophet and differed over what the messenger's extra commission was: a new law, or for Ibn Taymiyya a mission to a people who reject God. Abraham, whom critics list as a messenger without a book, has scrolls in the Quran.
messenger-to-every-nation: The Quran says God sent a messenger to every people, and critics ask where the prophets of the Germans and the French are. We give six answers. The Quran says it tells the stories of only some messengers (40:78). Those it names include men sent to Egyptians, Assyrians and the cities of the plain, so it records more than Hebrews and Arabs. The Bible has prophets and priests of God outside Israel, and Acts 14 says God left no nation without witness.
muhammad-and-the-hebrew-prophets: A common objection says Muhammad (peace be upon him) knew the names of the Hebrew prophets and little else. We give six answers from the Quran.
