It quotes the Psalms in 21:105, introduced by "We have written in the Zabur". It sets out Torah laws in 5:45 and 5:32 and Ezekiel's teaching on individual responsibility in 53:38. It names Jonah, one of the writing prophets, with his father's name and his story, and Elijah with his challenge over Baal. The Prophet also gave rules for hearing the earlier scriptures.
ishmael-in-the-quran-and-genesis: The Quran calls Ishmael a messenger and a prophet, and critics answer that he was a tribal chief given a prophetic role to supply Muhammad (peace be upon him) with an ancestor. We set out six facts. The Quran names him messenger and prophet in 19:54, has him teach prayer and alms and places him with Abraham at the Kaaba. Genesis does not call him a prophet, and records that God heard him, blessed him, was with him and promised him a great nation. Josephus called the Arabs his descendants.
scrolls-of-abraham: The Quran twice cites "the scriptures of Abraham and Moses", and Wikipedia reports three proposed sources for them: a Sabian book named in the Fihrist, the Sefer Yetzirah and the Testament of Abraham. We set out what the Quran says the scrolls taught, then read each candidate. The Fihrist's book is a ninth-century compilation that quotes the Quran, the Sefer Yetzirah is a cosmology of letters and numbers, and the Testament saves a soul by Abraham's intercession, against 53:38. None matches the Quran's description.
no-compulsion-in-religion: Critics say "There is no compulsion in religion" (2:256) is a lone verse, more liberal in appearance than in reality. We set out six facts. The verse was revealed to stop Muslim parents forcing their children out of Judaism and Christianity. Some early authorities called it abrogated, and al-Tabari recorded their view and rejected it. Malik, al-Awzai and the Hanafis extended protection beyond the People of the Book, and the first conquest of India extended it to Hindu temples. The principle recurs in 10:99, 18:29 and 88:22.
holy-war-in-the-bible: A familiar argument sets jihad against the Gospel and calls holy war a contradiction. We set out seven facts critics pass over. The Hebrew Bible commands total war against Canaanite cities and the Amalekites, women and children included, and records it at Jericho, Ai and Midian. The Psalms praise God as a warrior. Revelation describes the Word of God making war, and the Church proclaimed the Crusades as a penitential act with a spiritual reward. Both traditions have to account for sacred war.
septuagint: A standard reply to the Muslim claim of alteration says the Septuagint, translated before Christ, matches the Hebrew Bible exactly. We set out seven facts. The Septuagint shows that much of the text was stable before Christianity. Its contents differ: it adds Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and Maccabees. Its Jeremiah and Job are shorter, its Daniel and Esther longer, and its figures in Genesis, Exodus and Samuel differ. The New Testament quotes it where it departs from the Hebrew.
oldest-bible-codices: When Muslims say the Bible was altered, a common reply points to the codices Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and Alexandrinus as complete Bibles from before Islam. We set out eight facts. They are real Bibles from before Islam, and none is complete. Sinaiticus is split between four cities and includes Barnabas and Hermas, and Alexandrinus includes two letters of Clement. Both fourth-century codices end Mark at 16:8 and lack the adultery story, Sinaiticus carries some 23,000 corrections, and the two disagree with each other.
jamnia-and-the-hebrew-canon: A common claim says rabbis met at Jamnia about AD 90 and closed the Hebrew Bible. We set out six facts. The source behind the claim records a debate in a school about two or three books, written down generations later, with no council and no list. Writers on both sides of the Muslim and Christian conversation have leaned on the claim. An argument that depends on the Hebrew Bible closing at a known date in AD 90 needs another date or another argument.
earliest-new-testament-lists: When were the 27 books of the New Testament collected, and by whom? A common answer names a council or an emperor. We set out seven facts from the surviving lists, from Marcion to Athanasius and the councils of North Africa. Each list records what one writer or one region read. The books were gathered by use and argument over about three centuries, and councils later confirmed lists for their own churches. Anyone who asks which New Testament the Quran meant must read the lists, and they differ.
revelation-warning-and-the-canon: Revelation 22:18 to 19 warns against adding to or taking from "this book", and some Christian writers read it as a seal on the whole Bible that rules out the Quran. We set out five facts. The warning guards one book, the Revelation of John. It was written before the churches had assembled a Bible, and the list of books it would close was argued over for centuries after. The verse cannot carry the argument made from it.
disputed-books-of-the-new-testament: Every church today holds the same 27 New Testament books, and for centuries the churches did not agree on them. We set out six facts: which books were disputed, by whom and for how long, starting from Eusebius's categories in the early fourth century. The dispute ran from the second century to the Reformation, with the doubts strongest in the East and over a few books. Churches that now agree on the list reached it by different roads.
comma-johanneum: The King James Version reads at 1 John 5:7 that "the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one", and almost every modern translation omits it. We set out eight facts. The words are absent from every Greek manuscript before the fourteenth century and from the best early Vulgate manuscripts, and the Greek defenders of the Trinity never quote them. They first appear in Latin writers, entered the printed Greek through Erasmus in 1522, and a papal decree defended them in 1897.
old-testament-variant-readings: Some say that whatever is true of the New Testament, the Old has no variant readings at all. We set out eight examples from Jewish tradition itself. The Masoretic Text carries several hundred notes telling readers to read a word other than the one written, and rabbinic tradition lists eighteen places where scribes changed the text out of reverence. The Samaritan Pentateuch differs in some six thousand places, including Deuteronomy 27:4. The Dead Sea Scrolls restore a paragraph of 1 Samuel 11 and a verse of Psalm 145.
kings-and-chronicles-numbers: Chronicles retells Samuel and Kings, often word for word, and in places their figures disagree, as with Solomon's forty thousand or four thousand stalls. We set out eight points. The books disagree on stalls, ages, census totals, years of famine, prices, the capacity of the bronze Sea and the height of the temple pillars, and 2 Samuel 21:19 credits Elhanan with killing Goliath. The usual defence calls these copyist errors. A text with errors of transmission has been altered, whatever the cause.
genealogies-of-jesus: Matthew and Luke give Jesus two genealogies that agree to David and then divide. We set out eight points. They give Joseph different fathers and different lines from David, sharing almost no names between David and Joseph. Julius Africanus explained the difference by levirate marriage and admitted he could not prove it. The theory that Luke gives Mary's line appears in the fifteenth century and fits Luke's wording poorly, and Raymond Brown judged both lists to be Joseph's. Matthew omits four kings to reach his pattern.
bible-alteration-claim-before-islam: Christian replies often say that only Muslims accuse the Bible of corruption, and do so because Islam needs it. We give eight answers. The Talmud records a rabbi charging the Samaritans with falsifying their Torah. Justin Martyr accused the Jews of removing prophecies, Celsus said Christians rewrote the Gospel, Dionysius of Corinth and others accused rival Christians of falsifying scripture, and the Pseudo-Clementine Homilies taught that false passages had entered the Torah. The charge is old and was made before Islam.
revelatory-exegesis: A later revelation that tells what an earlier one meant is older than Islam, and scholars call it revelatory exegesis. We check eight examples from a debate on the Islamic dilemma against the texts. Daniel reads Jeremiah this way, Qumran reads Habakkuk, Paul reads Genesis and Exodus, and Matthew and Luke read Mark. A critic who calls the Quran false for doing the same must say why the method is allowed in those books. The Quran judges the earlier books as muhaymin and closes the series with a final prophet.
seal-of-the-prophets: In a debate a Christian granted that the Quran may reread the earlier books, and asked why Muslims should not reread the Quran in the light of Joseph Smith or Baha'u'llah. We give eight answers. The Quran names its messenger the seal of the prophets, the earliest commentators read that as the last, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) said there is no prophet after him. The Quran calls the religion complete and its text guarded. For anyone who accepts the Quran, its own words remove the condition for a later rereading.
covenant-of-the-prophets: A Christian debater argues that Quran 3:81, the covenant God took from the prophets, makes confirming the earlier scripture the test of a true messenger, and that the Quran fails it. We grade the points of that reading. The verse binds every prophet to believe in and help a messenger who comes confirming what God gave him. Al-Tabari reads it as a pledge passed to their peoples, and Ibn Kathir, with al-Suddi and Tawus, reads it as a pledge to Muhammad (peace be upon him). The report in Ali's name is weak, and the meaning stands without it.
ask-those-who-read-the-scripture: Quran 10:94 tells the Prophet that if he is in doubt he should ask those who read the scripture before him, and some read it as handing the final word to the Bible. We give six points from the surrounding verses and the earliest commentators. The verse is a conditional spoken to a Prophet who, by the early reports, neither doubted nor asked. It points to a narrow question and to named witnesses who believed. Read that way, it fits a Quran that confirms the earlier books and is their criterion.
torah-on-the-cushion-hadith: In a debate a questioner cited Abu Dawud 4449, in which the Prophet (peace be upon him) lays the Torah on a cushion and says he believes in it, and concluded that the Torah in Medina was the true one. We grade seven points. Al-Albani graded the report hasan, and Shu'ayb al-Arna'ut judged its wording weak, since one narrator alone tells it so. The event is firm in al-Bukhari and Muslim. Ibn Hajar reads the respect as respect for what God revealed to Moses, which leaves the copy's integrity an open question.
who-changed-the-bible: A questioner asked who could have changed every copy of the Bible when Christians copied it for centuries across many lands. We give nine answers. The change never had to reach every copy. The Gospels were written by unnamed authors and named later, six letters under Paul's name are judged by most critical scholars to be by others, Matthew reworded Mark as he wrote, and passages entered the text while copies were few. Ordinary copying did the rest. The process needed time and many hands, and no conspiracy.
muhammad-never-wrote-it-down: A questioner asked why anyone should trust the Quran or the hadith when Muhammad (peace be upon him), like Jesus, wrote nothing himself. We give seven answers. The Prophet had the Quran written by named scribes while he was present to correct them, a stronger chain than a book found decades after its author with no history. The hadith are a mixed record, and the Muslim scholars who sorted them were the first to say so. A questioner who presses that point is doing what those scholars did.
ransom-bible-quran: Mark 10:45 says the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many, and a doctrine of salvation rests on it. We grade eight points from the Bible and the Quran. The Quran answers with a rule it repeats: on the Last Day no ransom is taken and each soul carries its own load. Intercession by God's leave remains, and so does the ransom of Abraham's son, which saved an innocent and carried no sin. The Hebrew Bible stands closer to the Quran here than to the later doctrine.
will-every-non-muslim-go-to-hell: Many who leave Islam say the first crack was one question: what becomes of a kind neighbour who never accepted the message? We give seven points from the sources. The Quran says the religion God accepts is submission to Him, and classical scholars held that this is completed by accepting Muhammad (peace be upon him) once his message plainly reaches a person. The Quran also says God punishes no one before a messenger has come, names believing Jews, Christians and Sabians in its promises and tells all people not to despair of mercy.
jews-behind-the-stone-hadith: A report describes a battle at the end of time in which a stone or tree tells Muslims that a Jew hides behind it, and some cite it as proof that Islam is hostile to Jews by design. We give six points. The report is authentic by the standards of hadith. It is a prediction among the signs of the Hour, in the future tense, and gives no command for any present time. Against its use as a licence stand the Prophet's own dealings with Jews, his ban on killing women and children and the Quran's limits on fighting.
can-a-muslim-befriend-a-non-muslim: Some who leave Islam were taught that a Muslim must not befriend Jews and Christians, then met non-Muslims kinder than anyone at their mosque. We give six points on the verses behind the teaching. They are best read as being about alliance and patronage in a community at war, and some teachers read them more widely. The same book commands justice and kindness to those who do not fight (60:8), permits their food and marriage to their women, and tells believers to stay kind to a pagan parent.
women-in-hell-and-deficient-intelligence: Two lines from one sermon of the Prophet (peace be upon him), that most of the people of the Fire were women and that women are "deficient in intelligence and religion", are quoted more than almost any other. We give six points. The report is sound and its words are hard. Read whole, it is a feast-day sermon urging women to give, it names conduct as the cause of the warning, and it defines its two phrases by a rule of evidence and a lifting of prayer. The Quran promises men and women the same reward.
three-divorces-and-the-one-night-marriag: An account among former Muslims describes a man who divorces his wife three times in anger and pays another man to marry her for one night so he can take her back. We give six points from the sources. The Quran allows two reconcilable divorces and makes the third final, undone only by a real second marriage. The Prophet (peace be upon him) cursed the man who marries to make a woman lawful again and the one who arranges it. A woman can end a marriage, and her consent is required.
was-muhammad-a-narcissist: Some former Muslims argue that the orphaned Prophet (peace be upon him) grew into a narcissist who used religion for power. We give six points on this diagnosis of the dead. He was an orphan, as the Quran says, and the further details the argument adds are absent from the accounts we have read. The record shows a man who served his household, left nothing, refused credit for an eclipse and was corrected in public by the book he brought. That book has him disclaim power and knowledge of the unseen.
safiyya-and-the-women-captured-in-war: Some former Muslims say the marriage of Safiyya bint Huyayy, taken captive at Khaybar, was rape. We give six points from the sources. The sound reports say the Prophet (peace be upon him) freed her and made her freedom her dowry, waited until her period ended, consummated the marriage after three days on the road and defended her against a taunt. They record neither consummation on the day her husband died nor force. The deaths of her father and husband belong to the war at Khaybar.
what-former-muslims-testimonies-show: Collections of former Muslims' testimonies conclude that their pages reveal what Islam is. We give six points on what a testimony can show. It is strong evidence of what happened to the writer and what was taught where she lived, and those who suffered should be believed. It is weak evidence of what the religion teaches, since household, state and tribe stand between the sources and a life. A collection chosen from those who left cannot give rates, and the claim that the violent are the faithful cannot be tested by it.
when-a-stranger-online-calls-islam-a-cul: Online threads often call Islam a dangerous cult, a lie and a religion whose rules for women are primitive. We answer six such claims and describe a reply that works. Answer one claim, correct one fact, point to one source and leave the rest, without insult. Islam is no cult by the usual meaning of the word, belief cannot be forced by the Quran's own rule, its truth claims are open to evidence, and the verses on modesty state their reason.
nine-questions-from-the-floor-islamic-di: After a public debate on the Islamic dilemma, the audience asked short, direct and mostly fair questions about the Quran and the earlier scriptures. We answer nine of them from the sources. The Prophet's not writing is answered by the Companions' written copies. The Torah of the Quran has two senses that the verses keep apart. The readings of the Quran are, by the sources, variants the Prophet taught. Where the Muslim speaker's view differs from ours, on miracles, the reach of the hadith and the Quran's perfection, we say so.
jeremiah-new-covenant-hebrews-and-the-qu: Christian argument often uses "the new covenant" to say the first covenant was always meant to be replaced. We set out six points from Jeremiah 31, Hebrews and the Quran. Read alone, Jeremiah describes a renewal: the same law written on the heart, forgiveness without sacrifice and a people that remains. Hebrews reads it as a replacement. The Quran speaks of many covenants and reads the line of covenants as one religion renewed through each prophet. Renewal and replacement are different ideas, and the texts say which each tradition means.
what-the-pagans-of-mecca-said-about-alla: We ask what the people of Mecca themselves believed about Allah, from the Quran and the early reports, while noting that no text by a Meccan pagan survives. We give eight answers. The pagans knew Allah as the creator and called on Him in danger. They added partners and intermediaries, and the Quran's quarrel with them is over those additions. Nothing in the reports makes Allah a moon, and the Quran counts the moon among His creatures. The moon-god claim has no support in the sources.
sun-muddy-spring-and-fixed-earth: Critics say Quran 18:86, where Dhu al-Qarnayn finds the sun setting in a muddy spring, and a hadith about the sun prostrating beneath the Throne show a flat-earth author. We give six answers. The verse describes what the traveller saw, as the commentators explained centuries ago. The hadith, read beside the Quran's account of all creation bowing to God, speaks of obedience. The Bible and weather forecasts also speak of the sun rising and setting. The Quran points to the sun and moon as signs of order and sets out no model of the heavens.
authority-of-the-sunnah-quran-alone: Critics and a few Muslims say the hadith were collected late and include forgeries, so a believer should follow the Quran alone (6:38, 6:114). We give six answers. The hadith scholars knew of forgery first, and the chains, the books of fabricated reports and the grading of narrators exist because of it. The consistent position is critical acceptance: test each report, keep what passes and drop what fails. The Quran sends its reader to the Prophet (peace be upon him), and the community learned to pray from him.
did-the-quran-say-muhammad-sinned: The Quran tells the Prophet (peace be upon him) to seek forgiveness for his dhanb, rebukes him for frowning at a blind man and corrects his decisions, and critics ask how he can then be the model of 33:21. We give six answers on prophetic protection. The verses are real. They record corrections of judgement, and Muslim doctrine protects the prophets from grave sins and from error in conveying the message. The Bible attributes adultery, idolatry and drunkenness to prophets, and the Quran keeps every prophet free of those.
islam-and-evolution: Some atheist writers and some Muslim writers agree that the Quran's creation of Adam from clay rules out evolution, and draw opposite conclusions. We give seven answers. The texts fix one thing: Adam was created by God and given the spirit. Beyond that line they leave biology open, and the Quran invites the study of how creation began (29:20). Muslims disagree on the question, and the disagreement is real, as is the room the texts leave.
slander-against-mary: Quran 4:156 condemns some Jews for a great slander against Mary, and critics ask for evidence that anyone made such a charge before Islam. We give six answers. The written record shows the charge that Jesus was born of adultery from the second century to the sixth, in Celsus and in rabbinic sources. The Babylonian Talmud, taking its final shape in the same centuries as the Quran's revelation, contains the Pandera account. The Quran answered a slander current among the people it addressed.
uncreated-quran-and-the-logos: An argument going back to John of Damascus says that since Muslims hold the Quran to be God's eternal, uncreated Word, they should accept the Christian Word of John 1:1. Harry Wolfson called the Muslim idea "inlibration". We give six answers. The likeness is real, and it breaks at John 1:14: the Christian Logos is a person who becomes flesh. The Muslim position keeps Creator and creature apart. The eternal speech belongs to God, and every copy and recitation belongs to creation.
honour-killing-and-islamic-law: Critics say honour killings cluster in Muslim societies, that Muslim states excuse them and that the Prophet praised a man's jealousy. We give seven answers, separating what the Quran and the law require from custom and from imported penal codes. The Quran's procedure makes private killing a crime, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) refused a husband the sword. Honour killing is also documented among Hindu and Sikh families, and in Brazilian and Italian law. It is a crime of custom that the sharia condemns.
women-leading-prayer: Critics say Islam denies women religious authority because a woman may not lead men in prayer, citing the mixed Friday prayer in New York in 2005. We give six answers that separate two questions. The majority rule restricts one role in one act of worship. Women in the Muslim record taught, narrated hadith and gave rulings to men and women alike. The New Testament goes further, in 1 Timothy 2:12 and 1 Corinthians 14:34. The record of women's learning answers the wider charge.
oaths-in-the-quran: Many Meccan surahs open with oaths by the sun, the fig and the olive, the dawn and the winds, and critics argue that an author who swears by the sun is no god. We give five answers. In Arabic and in the Quran, an oath calls something to witness. Angelika Neuwirth and Devin Stewart show how the oath clusters set the theme and the rhyme and mark the turn to the claim. In the Bible God swears by Himself. An oath in the Quran calls creation to witness for its Creator.
is-the-cross-a-pagan-symbol: Muslim polemic often claims that the cross was a pagan emblem, held by Hindu and Egyptian gods and carved on Mithraic monuments, which the church took over. We test the claim in six points from the Church Fathers, the early papyri and the fourth- and fifth-century historians. The first Christian signs were the fish and the dove, the cross was a scandal, the gesture appears about 200 and the public emblem follows Constantine. Cross shapes predate Christianity, and the Coptic looped cross adapts the ankh. The longer lists of pagan crosses rest on nineteenth-century compilations without traceable sources.
jesus-prostrated-in-prayer: Many Christians regard prostration, the forehead on the ground, as a Muslim posture foreign to the worship of Jesus. We test that view in five passages. Matthew says Jesus fell on his face in Gethsemane; Genesis, Numbers and Psalm 95 show Abraham, Moses, Aaron and the congregation bowing to the ground; and the Roman and Orthodox rites still keep the full prostration. The posture belongs to biblical religion, and it shows Jesus as the Quran describes him: a servant who yields his will to God.
did-jesus-fast: Christian writers sometimes set the fixed fast of Ramadan against the freedom of the Gospel, citing Jesus' answer about the bridegroom in Mark 2. We give five facts. Jesus fasted forty days in the line of Moses and Elijah, taught his followers to fast in secret, and said they would fast once the bridegroom was taken from them; the Didache shows the first Christians keeping two fast days a week. The Quran places Ramadan in the line of those before. The rules of Lent and Ramadan differ, and their purpose is shared.
birth-of-jesus-in-surah-maryam: Critics call the Quran's account of the birth of Jesus a patchwork of the palm-tree legend of Pseudo-Matthew, an Arabic infancy gospel and a confusion of Mary with Miriam. We read Quran 19:16 to 36 in seven details beside Matthew, Luke and the later texts. Pseudo-Matthew may postdate the Quran, the infancy gospel's speaking child calls himself Son of God where the Quran's calls himself a servant, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) answered the question of the sister of Aaron in his lifetime. The passage interprets its own miracle.
jesus-and-the-sabbath: A familiar reading holds that Jesus broke the Sabbath and set his followers free of the Law of Moses, and it quotes John 5:18. We examine five Sabbath controversies in the Gospels against the Torah and the Jewish law of the time. Each turns on how the commandment is kept: whether plucking grain is reaping, whether a healing that could wait may be done. Jesus argues from the purpose of the Torah, and Nina Collins shows the debate was a Jewish one. The Quran describes him as confirming the Torah and lightening some of its rules.
original-sin: Christian preachers argue that every child of Adam is born guilty, so that Islam cannot see the need for a saviour; some Muslim writers reply that Augustine invented the doctrine. We answer six questions from the texts. Genesis records the consequences of Adam's sin, and Deuteronomy and Ezekiel deny inherited guilt. Cyprian shows the doctrine before Augustine, and the Catholic, Orthodox and Reformed churches still define it differently. The Quran tells of Adam's repentance and forgiveness, and teaches that each child is born upon the fitra.
does-god-require-blood-to-forgive: Christian apologists argue from Hebrews 9:22 that God forgives no sin without the shedding of blood, so that the death of Jesus is the only way to forgiveness. We test the claim against five passages. Leviticus 17:11 gives blood its place at the altar, yet Leviticus 5 forgives the poor man who brings flour. Hebrews 9:22 says nearly everything, and the Catholic bishops' note limits it to the cult. Psalm 51, Hosea 6:6, Ezekiel 18 and Jonah 3 tie forgiveness to repentance. The Bible does not teach that God is unable to forgive without blood.
islamic-repentance-and-christian-atoneme: Two caricatures shape debate: that Islam offers no assurance of forgiveness, and that Christians may sin freely because Jesus paid. We compare the traditions on six points from their own texts: the ground of forgiveness, the cross, inherited burden, grace, confession and restitution. The Quran, al-Nawawi, the Catholic Catechism, the Orthodox Church in America and the Westminster Confession all require sorrow, a changed life and repair of harm. The traditions divide on whether reconciliation with God rests on the death of Jesus or on God's direct acceptance of the repentant.
are-children-born-sinful: Reformed confessions hold that Adam's corrupted nature passes to every child. We set out five answers to whether a newborn is sinful. Islam teaches that every child is born upon the fitra and that the pen is lifted from him until puberty. The Catholic Catechism speaks of an inherited state without personal fault; the Orthodox deny the infant's guilt; Lutherans baptise infants, and Baptists speak of moral capacity. On children who die, the churches entrust them to mercy, and a hadith places them with Abraham. Islam holds that no child needs a saviour.
adam-and-eve-in-genesis-and-the-quran: Muslims often say the Bible blames Eve and the Quran does not; Christian critics say the Quran took its Adam story from earlier sources. We compare Genesis 2 to 3 with Quran 2, 7 and 20 on five points: whom the tempter addresses, how blame is shared, whether repentance is accepted, what the consequences mean, and whether guilt passes on. Later texts such as 1 Timothy 2:14 and Sirach 25:24 place the weight on the woman, while the Quran holds both to account and records their forgiveness. We also examine the hadith that names Eve.
jesus-the-word-of-god-in-the-quran: Christian apologists argue that the Quran's title for Jesus, a Word from God, confesses the divine Word of John 1. We examine six facts: the title is prepared in the story of John in 3:39; 3:45 names Jesus a Word from Him and 3:47 explains it by the command Be; Ibn Kathir reads it the same way; 4:171 sets the title beside messenger and forbids saying Three; John's Word is God made flesh; and the Quran uses word of much besides Jesus. The Quran's context gives the title its meaning.
sam-shamoun-under-oath: Sam Shamoun, a prolific critic of Islam, asks his readers to accept his reading of sources they cannot check. We test his own reliability against the two 2020 opinions of the Appellate Court of Illinois in his divorce case, quoting the court exactly. The trial court found his testimony on income inconsistent and not credible, traced donations and income he did not disclose, recorded his failures to comply with orders, a discovery sanction and an order of protection, and called his plea of poverty disingenuous. We also state the point on which his appeal succeeded.
jesus-sign-of-the-hour: Christian apologists argue that Quran 43:61, which calls Jesus knowledge of the Hour, gives him a divine attribute. We examine five points: the surrounding passage, which calls Jesus a servant who says my Lord and your Lord; al-Tabari's record of the two referents of the pronoun, Jesus or the Quran; the readings ilm, knowledge, and alam, sign, with Ubayy's reminder; Ibn Kathir's preference for Jesus' descent; and the Quran's denial of his divinity in 5:72 to 75. A sign of the Hour points to God and shares nothing of His divinity.
sons-of-god-in-the-bible: Christian preachers argue that because the Bible calls Jesus the Son of God, it teaches that he is God. We set out seven biblical uses of the title: the heavenly court in Job, the disputed sons of Genesis 6, Israel as firstborn, the Davidic king, peacemakers and believers, Adam in Luke 3:38, and Jesus himself. In John 10 Jesus defends the title by citing Psalm 82 and calls himself one sanctified and sent. The title marks a relation to God, and the Quran answers every claim of divine sonship alike.
ezekiel-twenty-three-allegory: Ezekiel 23 is cited by Muslim speakers for its explicit verses, and Christian apologists answer that it is an allegory. We examine five facts: the chapter names Samaria and Jerusalem as the two sisters, their lovers are the empires of Assyria, Babylon and Egypt, its charge is idolatry and the sacrifice of children, its wording is explicit and softened in translation, and Christian and Jewish scholars such as Bibb and van Dijk-Hemmes object to its imagery. We honour the prophetic message and measure the wording against the Quran's restraint.
ezekiel-twenty-three-in-malay-and-indone: Some say the Malay and Indonesian Bibles hide the explicit verses of Ezekiel 23; others say the wording quoted by Muslims is not in their Bible. We compare Ezekiel 23:17 and 23:20 in six editions on the SABDA parallel Bible: Terjemahan Lama, Terjemahan Baru, Bahasa Indonesia Sehari-hari, Alkitab Yang Terbuka, Shellabear 2011 and Alkitab Versi Borneo. Formal versions keep the Hebrew images, the everyday version paraphrases them, and no edition removes the verse. A Bible read in Malay or Indonesian is a translation shaped by its committee.
biblical-anthropomorphism: Christian apologists reply to Muslim criticism of biblical anthropomorphism that the Quran also speaks of God's hands, face and throne. We examine six Torah passages in which God walks in the garden, regrets, goes down to learn, wrestles Jacob, rests and is refreshed, and is seen face to face. The Bible's own correctives in Numbers 23:19, 1 Samuel 15:29 and Exodus 33:20 deny them, and Maimonides read them as figures. The Quran affirms God's attributes without asking how and measures every description by 42:11.
camel-method: The Camel Method, set out by Southern Baptist missionary Kevin Greeson in 2004, asks Muslims to read Quran 3:42 to 55 as a bridge to the New Testament. We examine six facts: its origin in South Asia, its name and three points, what the passage says of Jesus, the explanation in 3:59 that al-Tabari ties to the Najran delegation, the Christian critics who called it heresy and deception, and the conversion figures that rest on the missionaries' own word. Read whole, the passage leads to the worship of God alone.
quran-passages-in-christian-missions: Christian missionaries argue that Quranic verses on Jesus point beyond Islam. We examine five passages and the writers who use them: Surah Al Imran 3:42 to 55 in the Camel Method, a Word from Him in 3:45, a spirit from Him in 4:171 as Sam Shamoun reads it, the miracles of 5:110, and the command in 10:94 as the Jesus-Islam site reads it. In each case the surrounding verses answer the argument: the same phrase in 58:22 describes believers, and the miracles come by God's leave.
does-the-virgin-birth-make-jesus-divine: Christian writers such as Don Stewart argue that a fatherless birth shows Jesus to be more than human. We examine five answers: Christian writers of standing do not rest his deity on the birth, the Quran answers Mary's question with the command Be, Adam had neither father nor mother and Luke calls him the son of God, the infant Jesus calls himself a servant in Surah Maryam, and Mary and her son form one sign. The Quran affirms the miracle and denies the inference.
principles-of-dawah-in-the-quran: The Quran sets rules for the manner of inviting others to Islam as well as its content. We examine six principles from the verses and their commentators: wisdom, good counsel and the better argument in 16:125 as al-Tabari reads it, no compulsion in 2:256 and 10:99 with al-Faruqi's conditions of the call, real common ground in 3:64, the better way of disputing in 29:46, no insult to what others worship in 6:108, and guidance left to God in 28:56. The invitation keeps its truth claim and is made freely.
religious-pluralism-and-islam: The question whether Islam accepts religious pluralism joins five questions into one. We separate them: diversity as God's will set against a claim of equal truth in 5:48, justice to peaceful neighbours in 60:8, dialogue on common terms without surrender in 3:64 and 29:46, the salvation verses 2:62 and 3:85 as Ibn Kathir, Lumbard and Sirry read them, and the difference between a doctrine of salvation and a verdict on a person. Islam protects and invites the followers of other faiths without holding every religion true.
was-jesus-born-on-christmas-day: Two claims meet every December: that 25 December is the birthday of Jesus, and that Christmas is a renamed pagan festival. We examine six facts: the Gospels give no date, Clement of Alexandria recorded dates in April and May, the Chronography of 354 attests a Roman feast on 25 December, historians weigh a calculation theory against a festival theory, the East kept 6 January until the Roman date spread from Constantinople after 380, and the birthday remains unknown. Neither claim survives the evidence, and the Quran directs attention to the meaning of the birth.
christmas-quran-jesus-birth: The Christmas card merges Matthew and Luke into one scene, and comparisons with the Quran often start from the card. We compare Surah Maryam with the two Gospels on five points: who receives the news of the birth, where and how Mary gave birth, who comes to see the child, the infant's speech from the cradle in 19:30 to 33, and what the birth is said to mean. The three accounts agree on the virgin conception by God's command and differ on its setting, its witnesses and its meaning, which the Quran gives as servanthood and prophethood.
christmas-traditions-historical-origins: The claim that Christmas is pagan, and the reply that every custom is biblical, both pass over the records. We trace six customs to their sources: the decorated tree in Strasbourg in 1605, the crib scene with Francis of Assisi at Greccio in 1223, gift-giving centuries before Dickens, Santa Claus from the bishop of Myra through Sinterklaas and the poem of 1823, the carol Hark! The Herald Angels Sing from 1739 to 1855, and the greenery from Pliny's Druids to Wichern's Advent wreath of 1839. Only the mistletoe has a pagan record behind it.
can-muslims-say-merry-christmas: Muslims are told either that every scholar forbids Christmas greetings or that none ever objected. We set out five positions with their reasons: Ibn al-Qayyim's prohibition of congratulation on religious rites, Ibn Uthaymin's application of it to Christmas, contemporary scholars who permit the greeting as courtesy, Egypt's Dar al-Ifta on 60:8 and 4:86, and the guidelines of Malaysia's National Fatwa Committee of 2007 and the Federal Territories Mufti. The disagreement is real and recognised, and every position commands justice and kindness to peaceful neighbours.
former-christian-ministers-who-embraced-: Christian critics charge that lists of clergy who embraced Islam inflate their titles, and many lists do. We present five cases whose former Christian role is documented: David Benjamin Keldani, archpriest of Urmia, from the Brill bibliographical history; Yusuf Estes, a Texas preacher; Jerald Dirks, an ordained United Methodist deacon; Kenneth Jenkins, a Pentecostal minister and elder; and Idris Tawfiq, a Catholic priest who left the priesthood before becoming Muslim. Each is given at the strength of its sources, and a conversion is treated as testimony to a free choice.
